EntertainmentTab.title: The perfect books for the beach … picked by Freida McFadden, Mick Herron, Robert Harris and more
EntertainmentTab.text:
It is important to follow a balanced diet on holiday. Too many “My Wife’s Sister’s Husband’s Psychopath”, and you’ll get confused and grumpy. Too much sugary romance and your teeth will fall out. Something too big and challenging you’ve been meaning to get round to for ages will make you feel guilty and more liable to give in to scrolling, and if you take too many supposedly upmarket “must reads” of the summer, you will simply prove to yourself just how much overhyped averageness there is out there, when all you want is something satisfying.

You need to be able to chop and change depending on your mood, which means fiction and nonfiction. And finally, you need to be able to throw all of these rules out of the window if you find a sandy old water-stained copy of, for example, James Herbert’s Domain in your holiday cottage and decide to devote yourself to 600 pages of post-nuclear mutant rat-strewn London, or choose to go for a full-on Maeve Binchy sesh.

My top tips for this summer? For the outward journey: Kathy Burke’s smash-hit and brilliant autobiography A Mind of My Own, a reminder of the absolute Britishness you are leaving behind. For that first post-rosé afternoon when you are filled with warmth and benevolence towards the world and everyone in it: Whistler by Ann Patchett.

For a wonderful immersive epic where everyone is also extremely boiling hot all the time: This Is Where the Serpent Lives by Daniyal Mueenuddin. For cruising altitude day four when everyone else has gone to see some stupid boring hot cave and left you alone and you want something quality and capable of being finished in an afternoon: Glorious Exploits by Ferdia Lennon. For the day everyone is doing your head in: Emma Cline’s huge hit from a couple of years ago, The Guest, a thoroughly nasty piece of work and the best of all those “neighbourhood psycho” books.

Nonfiction palate cleanser day: OK, everyone is going to be reading the Maggie Haberman Trump book, but for the love of God could we possibly not think about him for one solitary five-second interval? That would be the definition of a holiday. If annoying Americans are still your bag, try Belle Burden’sStrangers, about a seemingly perfect, rich Wasp marriage unexpectedly going down the toilet.

For queueing at non-EU passport control and cursing Nigel Farage’s £5m: The Impossible Fortune by Richard Osman. Forget the motley crew of celebrity impersonators that squelched along in his wake; Osman’s lightness of touch and genuine comic ability means this slips down more easily than free limoncello. Bonnes vacances!

author of The Housemaid

One of my favourite reads of the year has been TheCalamity Club by Kathryn Stockett. I’ve been on a historical kick lately, and this novel set in the southern US during the Great Depression is historical fiction at its best. The audiobook is masterfully narrated and by the last chapter, I had tears in my eyes.

author of Yesteryear In The Shampoo Effect by Jenny Jackson a group of friends in their mid-30s in a tight-knit Massachusetts coastal town deal with secrets, romance and the fallout from a stunning betrayal. It’s frothy and clever and perfect for a vacation.

Taffy Brodesser-Akner

author of Fleishman Is in Trouble I brought Here in the Dark by my New York Times colleague Alexis Soloski on vacation a couple of years ago. I couldn’t put it down from the minute I started it, even missing a family dinner so I could continue reading. (Sorry, kids!) It’s a modern noir about an acerbic theatre critic who finds herself caught up in a mystery, and I can’t say enough about its voice, its humour, its darkness, its poignancy and the twists and turns that make it a truly original thriller. I loved it.

author of Heartstopper

Convenience Store Woman by Sayaka Murata is about a woman whose only dream is to work at a convenience store and, like much of Murata’s work, explores the inner world of a woman who feels deeply uncomfortable about the role she’s forced into by society. It’s short, it’s strange, it’s the perfect read for a trip away this summer – and a great introduction to Murata, if you haven’t dipped in before.

author of the Slough House series

Beaches are for walking along not reading on, but when the paddling’s done and a sand-free environment’s been found, Daniel Mason’s Country People is a treat. A failed academic and his family relocate to Vermont, where his PhD avoidance strategies involve increasingly alarming immersion in local folklore. An absurd, joyful delight.

author of The Maid

The Paper Palace by Miranda Cowley Heller. August heat, a summer cabin in Cape Cod, and the unravelling of one woman’s secrets. Elle is happily married with three kids, but her whole life is upended by an illicit encounter with a childhood friend. A charged generational saga about love, desire and loss – you’ll need regular dips in the water to cool yourself as you read.

author of None of This Is True

The best page-turner I’ve read this year is It’s Not What You Think by Clare Mackintosh. She already lays claim to one of the genre’s greatest twists in her 2011 hit I Let You Go and here Mackintosh is back to deliver multiple twists, short chapters and non-stop reveals in this scintillating read.

author of Call Me by Your NameLondon Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe is about a 19-year-old Londoner who desperately wants to join the world of super-wealthy Russian oligarchs, many of whom live in the capital. He manages to affect belonging to that class until he is finally exposed for who he really is – a smart, resourceful but hapless kid. The story is totally addictive, real, and I couldn’t put it down.

author of The Guest List

The Wedding People by Alison Espach is an absorbing, transporting book that left me with a serious what-to-pick-next panic after finishing it. I took it on holiday last year and the summer setting makes it perfect: the waterfront hotel, the excursions on boats and in open-top cars, and also the unfurling sense of optimism. It’s a paean to solo travel, to leaving it – quite literally in this case – all behind. But it’s also a book with teeth, poignancy, depth and humanity, all qualities I look for in a top-notch summer read.

author of The Night Stairs

The Pinnacle by Abir Mukherjee is a satirical thriller set in a Mumbai skyscraper. A washed-up American actor is accused of killing his Bollywood starlet wife. It’s got everything you could want from a book: belly laughs, unforgettable characters, a thumping plot and simmering political rage.

author of the Ninth House series

The Last Baron by Tom Sancton. Thick with loathsome individuals and rich with history, this heavily researched story of a 1970s kidnapping in Paris spans generations. It is wildly juicy, just be prepared for a Succession experience: you’ll struggle to find anyone to root for but you won’t be able to look away.

author of The Midnight Library

The Infinite Sadness of Small Appliances by Glenn Dixon is a weird, wonderful book about a vacuum cleaner that becomes sentient after hearing To Kill a Mockingbird read aloud. Said vacuum cleaner renames herself Scout and embarks on a quest to save the human she lives with. It’s highly original and feels like a sign that – in the age of AI – the way out is through vivid human creativity.

author of The Names A will-they-won’t-they romance is a much-anticipated holiday treat for me, and Annabel Monaghan’s are guaranteed to make my cheeks ache from smiling and keep me reading until 2am. In Nora Goes Off Script, screenwriter and single mum Nora falls for a leading actor when her house is co-opted as a film location.

author of Conclave Graham Greene has accompanied me on a lot of holidays over the years, especially the novels set in hot climates. I recommend in particular The Power and the Glory, The Honorary Consul and The Quiet American – perfect reading for a sweltering beach, a deserted baggage hall, or a night-time veranda with a sickly blue light zapping the insects.

author of Yellowface

I recently read and loved Anthony Doerr’s Cloud Cuckoo Land. Like David Mitchell’s Cloud Atlas, it’s a testament to ridiculous hope and the power of stories that is also ridiculously, formally ambitious – its crosscutting storylines span centuries and continents. It’s precisely the kind of book I needed to remind me how high human storytelling can soar.

author of On We Go

An MP has been murdered and a taunting message left in binary code: “Catch me if you can.” So begins Body of Lies, the politically and technically prescient conclusion to Jo Callaghan’s unique Midlands-set series featuring Kat and Lock, a human and AI detective pairing. Brimful of big ideas and heart, its action-packed finale is, to put it mildly, as moving as it is thrilling.

author of Claws Out!

The Enchanted April by Elizabeth von Arnim. I read this recently and found it completely charming and brilliantly transporting. Four women, bored, lost, lonely and miserable respectively, take a villa in Italy for a month of respite. It’s funny, tender and trots along at pace. But above all else, it’s a novel about women and the community that springs up between them. A perfect beach read.

author of American Wife

Crash Into Me by Robinne Lee is the ideal beach read not just because I literally was reading it on the beach earlier this week, though I was, or because the American cover features waves crashing on the sand, but because it’s an irresistible mix of glamorous, thought-provoking and sexy. Jamaican-born, New York‑raised, France-dwelling photographer Cecilia is living temporarily with her famous director husband and kids in LA when she reconnects with Anouk, a model with whom she had a complex encounter 20 years earlier. Now the two women are middle-aged and equally tempted to protect and blow up their lives. This is Lee’s follow-up to The Idea of You, and it’s just as juicy.

author of Witch Trial

Nonesuch by Francis Spufford is an absolute banger. Historical meets fantastical in this London blitz-set novel. The perfect combination of literary and compulsive page-turner, it reads like a dream. A bonus recommendation for Time to Burn by Ellery Lloyd, which also starts in the blitz but adds a thoroughly contemporary, compelling time-travelling twist.

author of The Burning Grounds

My choice is The Shadow Step by Mark Billingham, the latest in the Blackpool-set series featuring the wisecracking, ballroom-dancing detective Declan Miller. This one sees our hero running an investigation into the murder of a rather despicable young man, which quickly gets derailed by the kidnapping of a student. As with the others in this series, Billingham weaves a fiendish plot but also lets rip with the jokes. An absolute joy to read.

author of The Death of Us

I’d recommend Main Characters by Bobby Palmer. Seb and Clara meet in a Soho square, and an epic on-again, off-again romance begins. But their story is narrated by everybody except the main characters. Sometimes it’s a close friend, but we also hear from people‑watchers, neighbours and colleagues. The result has the feeling of a short-story collection, with small, perceptive insights into a vast cast of characters, and the ways lives collide and divert. Make sure you have sunglasses to hand – I wept.

author of The Barbecue at No 9

This year, Dead Heat by Sabine Durrant exceeded my unofficial “beach read” criteria of 1) page-turning crime or thriller 2) set in hot weather. This elevated psychological thriller, which takes place over a Greek summer, gave me serious Patricia Highsmith vibes. It’s classy, cinematic and truly thrilling.

author of Getting Away With Murder In Five by Ilona Bannister, someone on a London train platform will die in five minutes when the train arrives. As the clock ticks down, you meet the characters who might die, and you get to know them intimately. If you want a completely immersive read, this is for you.

author of Karla’s Choice If Lewis Carroll sat down with Mick Herron to write a thriller about memory and nightmare, you’d get There Is No Antimemetics Division by qntm. A funny, gripping and genuinely disturbing counter-espionage monster novel told in beach-friendly episodic style. What’s not to love?

author of The Girl on the Train

Four Terrible Parents by Calla Henkel. Careering towards 40, two rock stars, an artist and a former banker decide the time has come to settle down, get married, and co-parent a child (while also renovating a hotel in South Carolina). Henkel’s comedy-slash-thriller is so fiendishly plotted you might not even notice all she has to say about art, love, friendship and family.

author of The Map of Bones

Recently reissued, Fenny by Lettice Cooper – first published in 1953 – is a coming-of-age story set in the Tuscan hills. Dripping with heat, the sound of cicadas and the smell of the pine trees, this is the story of a Yorkshire governess who pitches up at a villa outside Florence in the years before the second world war and falls in love with the country, the light, the Italian pace of life. Heartwarming, atmospheric, a perfect summer read.

author of Just My Luck

Mad Mabel by Sally Hepworth. You may not have heard of this Australian-born, New York Times bestselling author yet, but I’ve been reading her for years; I love everything she’s written and I’m waiting to see her to blow-up here. Her bittersweet, thrilling dramas are shot through with life-enhancing humour. Somehow Hepworth’s Aussie sunshine floods off the page even when she’s delivering dark twists and murders. In this novel, unapologetically grumpy, fiercely independent 81-year-old Elsie lives quietly in an Australian suburb, except everywhere she goes people die in mysterious circumstances.

author of All In I couldn’t get enough of Some Bright Nowhere by Ann Packer, which is told from the perspective of a husband whose terminally ill wife asks him to move out so her best friends can move in. The literary equivalent of a friend telling an increasingly shocking story, it’s an unexpected and deeply moving read.

GeneralTab.title: Fleeing a wall of flames: Tourists describe France wildfires escape
GeneralTab.text:
Families have relived how their tranquil holidays in France turned into a race to escape raging wildfires.

Tourists told the BBC of emergency alerts in the middle of the night, desperate drives just metres from six-storey high flames and the sight of people flocking to beaches with their suitcases.

Huge forest fires in south-west France and central Spain have displaced more than 220,000 people, with the French military drafted in to help and the Spanish government declaring a national emergency.

Winds and continued heat are still helping to fan the flames with some tourists reporting smelling acrid smoke like a "bonfire" far outside the affected areas.

Flights to Bordeaux and Madrid, the closest cities to the blaze-hit regions, are currently not affected. Earlier on Saturday, a French foreign minister described the fires as a "tragedy" but urged tourists not to cancel their travel plans.

Among those caught up in the crisis is Zac Morrison, who arrived in Cap Ferret - a popular peninsula blanketed with pine trees 40 miles (65km) south-west of Bordeaux - on Thursday.

The 21-year-old from London, who is on holiday with 10 members of his family, woke up to two text alerts at 04:00 and 06:00 local time ordering him to evacuate "by all means necessary".

"We had the gendarmerie [French military] going door to door," he told BBC Your Voice. "It was something like out of a movie - we had to take everything."

Since experiencing "panic" before a "well organised" operation to clear out the entire peninsula, he said he received four different evacuation alerts from the authorities - the most recent at 17:00 on Friday - after "we moved away from one fire to only get put into the crosshairs of another".

His family took shelter on a beach in nearby Arcachon before a relative came to their aid with a place to stay. His brother Nate, 11, is still coming to terms with having seen the flames.

"Other people have been sleeping in schools and warehouses and the beaches have had people just waiting for the go ahead," Morrison added. "There's people on the beach here with their suitcases."

He said the family was awaiting instructions on whether they can continue their holiday until mid August.

"It rained last night but we are hearing that electricity may be cut out over the peninsula, especially as the ash clouds go towards Bordeaux... I've heard about houses burning in just an hour, it's scary but sadly people here are getting used to it."

David Morton had enjoyed most of his week-long trip to Cap Ferret with his wife and two teenage sons in the forests under baking sun.

But the mixture of "tinder dry" pine and intense heat helped upend things on day five when the family was awoken on Friday morning.

"Our phones were all flashing and bleeping; there was a message saying we had to evacuate immediately and drive on the one road out of the [Cap Ferret] peninsula," he said.

"We literally threw everything into our suitcases and within 15 minutes were in the hire car."

He said they came within 500m of the main fire. "The flames were higher than full-size forest pine trees, so five or six storeys high, and it was clear this was a fire that was out of control at that point."

The family has stayed with friends until their flight home from Bordeaux on Saturday.

Others are still stranded. Rebecca Papin, a French-American visiting her holiday home in the commune of Biscarrosse, near to the Cap Ferret peninsula, saw a large plume of smoke in the distance on Thursday.

Just three hours later when she arrived home that night, "there were water planes in the sky dropping water, firefighter helicopters in the sky and the entire distance was just a wall of flames," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

"It was quite far away from my house but I could see it very clearly from the upstairs level of my home."

She said the authorities appeared "overwhelmed with trying" to fight the fire and issued no evacuation order, so she slept alongside her young children with her earplugs in - meaning she missed the sound of the evacuation overnight.

"When I woke up in the morning we were almost alone in the city because the city has been evacuated and I'm still here," she said.

"The main roads are closed because they're on fire - the police advised me on Friday at 07:30 to stay in my home, to not leave my home under any circumstance; there was ash falling from the sky like snow."

Some British families told the BBC they had moved 100 miles away to other parts of France to continue their holidays.

Mark Dorey, from Leeds, decided to drive to the Dordogne with his wife and three children after being evacuated from a campsite near Parentis-en-Born.

"You wouldn't believe it, but me and my two boys were watching a Queen tribute act at the campsite bar - straight after a rendition of Bohemian Rhapsody someone stopped them to say we were being evacuated at about 22:00," he said.

Before heading to the Dordogne the family spent a night with hundreds of other evacuees in a gymnasium.

He said he feels lucky to be looked after and safe, but is thinking about holidaying "closer to home" next year.

And BBC South's Joanna Kent, who was on holiday in the Cap Ferret peninsula earlier this week, recalled seeing her campsite deserted after two van loads of police told tourists they had 30 minutes to get out.

While the wildfires show no sign of abating soon, the UK Foreign Office is currently not advising against travel to France or Spain.

Éléonore Caroit, France's minister for international partnerships, advised tourists on Saturday: "You have entire areas that are fine, you're seeing similar phenomena in Spain and other countries.

"I'm in Paris and nothing is happening, and most other regions are OK, so do please come to France and do not cancel your travel plans.

"But wherever you are, please do be advised as to what might be happening."

In Madrid the fires are in the wider region far outside the city centre - and authorities are battling to stop different fires merging.

But the flames have already shut down a facility for US space agency Nasa 37 miles (65km) west of the city.

Madrid's regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso described the fire there as the "worst fire in the history of the region", with the area facing a "perfect storm" of high temperatures, relentless wind and merging fire fronts.

GeneralTab.title: Gangs, violence and dumped dead animals: The hidden world of illegal hare hunts
GeneralTab.text:
On a remote Cambridgeshire farm, where his nearest neighbour is half a mile away, Mathew Latta was making lunch when the peace was shattered by the sound of loud exhausts.

Latta ran to the window to see a convoy of more than a dozen 4x4s heading towards his farm. His iron gates were cut open with an angle grinder and concrete blocks were shifted out of the way to clear the convoy's path.

The vehicles drove right over his fields at speed, tearing up the crops and skirting the fence by the family's garden. Then more than 70 people got out of the vehicles, men dressed in military fatigues and balaclavas, cheering and playing music.

Dogs were brought out on leads and began to hunt hares.

"They were all stood up on their cars with binoculars," says Latta. "I would say this is 100% a properly organised coursing event, with competitors and competitive dogs. People watching the course - and watching and betting on that sport. It was quite terrifying."

Warning: This story contains images of dead animals

Latta and his family were trapped in their home. They kept calling the police, but nobody came. His daughter, then aged seven, was terrified and kept asking: "Are these men gonna come inside, daddy?"

More than three hours later, the bloodsport was finally over and the crowd dispersed. They left behind four cars, one of them a burnt-out wreck. It emerged that, earlier that day, the convoy had rampaged through an area 20 miles (32km) long in the county, forcing other cars off the road and even robbing a petrol station.

This is the modern reality of hare coursing. It is an ancient sport where dogs such as greyhounds or lurchers are used to hunt hares, which the coursers usually scare out from the wild. Points are awarded for the number of times the dogs force the hare to twist and turn as it runs - as well as for the kill.

The sport reached a peak of popularity in the 19th Century, but went underground after it was banned in the UK in 2005.

We began investigating this underworld for the BBC Radio 4 podcast Dead Rabbit after the bodies of dead hares and other animals were mysteriously dumped in two picturesque Hampshire villages in 2024.

In Awbridge, more than 20 carcasses - mostly hares and rabbits, along with a muntjac deer with a severed head - were strewn outside a primary school. Children were in tears when they arrived for lessons and found a horror-movie scene.

About seven miles north, in Broughton, about 50 hares were scattered near the entrance of the village's community shop, with blood smeared on the doors and a dead barn owl and kestrel tied to the door handles.

There have been almost 9,000 reports of hare coursing across the UK in the past three years, according to police responses to Freedom of Information Act requests by the BBC.

The figures are not definitive - some incidents may have been reported more than once, while others may not have been reported at all - but in the absence of official crime figures for illegal hare coursing, they give us an indication of the scale of the problem.

Cambridgeshire Constabulary says it was "very stretched" on the January day last year when Mathew Latta's farm was invaded, and the force says it did not respond the way it would have wanted. Supt Ben Martin tells us that the coursers had rampaged through the county deliberately, to distract police and send them to the wrong places.

Having been caught out, the force stepped up its efforts to investigate who was behind the illegal event, eventually arresting more than 40 people and charging 25, several of whom have now been convicted.

As officers tracked down the coursers, it turned out they had come from all over the country: Lincolnshire, Leicestershire, Berkshire, north Wales. "People had come hundreds of miles to be there that day," says Martin. "It was a proper operation."

Then, after searching an address belonging to one of the arrested men, police found the trophy the coursers had been competing for - the Super 8 Cup, etched with images of dogs and hares, standing maybe 2ft (61cm) tall, about the size of the FA Cup.

The invasion of Latta's farm had been a highlight of the illegal hare coursing calendar, a recurring cup competition whose previous winners are engraved on the base of the trophy - both the owners and the dogs, which had names such as "Beyoncé" and "Bunny".

A scene after the cup final last year, captured on video obtained by the BBC, shows how hare coursing involves serious money. A group of eight men can be seen drinking pints in a pub and shouting, as they haggle over a lurcher standing on the table before them. The dog was the Super 8 Cup champion of 2025 and sold for £55,000.

It is not the only evidence of the cash that flows through the illegal bloodsport: we were told the Super 8 Cup prize was about £50,000, while the entry fee for the competition was £1,000, as revealed by a seized phone belonging to one of the kingpins. Police say this cash funds the prize money and covers expenses, such as a pool of vehicles and even court costs in case the hare coursers are raided.

Ch Insp Kevin Lacks-Kelly, head of the UK National Wildlife Crime Unit, tells the BBC that money had also flowed into the illegal sport through livestreams for gamblers in China on one or two occasions. But he says the gangs in the UK did not need overseas bets to fund their illicit hobby.

Hare coursers were linked to crimes involving significant sums of money, says Lacks-Kelly, not "minimum-wage crimes". "Some of these lads are making a fortune. You've got some of the country's best organised criminals," he adds.

There are some localised events that still just involve a handful of men and dogs, Lacks-Kelly says, but the level of organisation in bigger events "has increased tenfold" with the influx of organised crime.

"They've got the advantage in numbers. And they will go anywhere and do anything and commit this crime at all costs," he says.

"They're like a small army, just do what they want, don't they? Turn up en masse, block roads off, drive over fields, cause damage, dump the cars, burn the cars out. Mass participation events that are designed to overwhelm."

The BBC contacted members of the Country Land and Business Association, which represents 30,000 rural landowners and businesses in England and Wales, to ask about their experiences with hare coursing.

About 50 responded, nearly all of them saying their land or property had been damaged. Someone in Cheshire said it happened every week, a farmer in Essex said it had happened more than 100 times, while one in North Yorkshire said 150 times.

And 29 of the respondents said they had been threatened with violence.

According to the survey responses, hare coursers had threatened to kidnap farmers' dogs, shouted that they would burn their buildings down, had thrown bricks through windows, made anonymous phone threats to stab them in the neck, used catapults to fire ball-bearings at them, rammed and damaged vehicles with people inside, and warned the farmers that they knew where they lived and where their kids go to school.

Wiltshire farmer David Lemon showed us his 3,000-acre farm, where hare coursers have previously torn up the fields with miles of tyre tracks. He has tried to fortify the land, closing off gateways, putting in concrete blocks or piles of logs, and digging rows of deep ditches to make it undrivable. But they still get in and, when he has tried to confront them, he has been threatened.

One gamekeeper was run over and badly injured when he tried to confront hare coursers on land he managed, says Tim Weston from the National Gamekeepers' Organisation.

"He broke both his legs, pelvis, ruptured lungs." Weston says. "They left at high speed, potentially could have left him for dead." Fortunately, the man is now back and work and recovering, he said.

As we talked, it turned out that Weston, who is now based in Wiltshire, grew up in a village near Broughton in Hampshire, where the animals were dumped outside the shop. In 2024, he was working in deer management on an estate where he suspects the dead hares had been killed.

The night before they were dumped, there had been wheel marks across the estate, he says. The local gamekeeper had stopped the hare coursers three or four times.

Weston says the abandoned animals were a message to say: "We've been. You didn't catch us this time."

Using dead animals to taunt landowners is common, Weston says. In our survey of farmers and landowners, 35 of the respondents said animal bodies had been deliberately left on their land.

It is a message to the local community that "we can do what we want because no-one's going to police it", Weston says.

Hampshire Police did arrest a man over the dumped animals at Broughton community shop, however. The force commissioned a forensic analysis of the dead kestrel and barn owl left on the doors and took DNA samples. James Kempster, a man who police say had a prior record of wildlife crimes, was arrested as a result.

At trial, Kempster denied he had abandoned the animals. CCTV footage of two men casually tossing dozens of dead hares outside the shop - one of them ripping one of the bodies in half to smear its blood around - were not clear enough to reveal their identities.

Kempster was convicted of handling the dead birds, a crime in itself because they are protected species. But he was found not guilty of criminal damage - the charge that related to abandoning the carcasses.

So was the incident really a warning or a taunt to the local community from hare coursers? With the perpetrators still unidentified, their motive cannot be known for certain.

One police officer recalls an arrangement of dead animals' whose message seemed undeniable, however. He tells us how he had sometimes found bodies strung over speed limit signs and street furniture in villages or left outside people's houses.

Once, he says, he had seen them laid out in the road, the corpses spelling out the words: "Catch me".

GeneralTab.title: Long overdue, life-changing or frivolous? Your thoughts on wedding rule changes
GeneralTab.text:
The day Sam and Courtney Scholey became husband and wife didn't feel like their wedding day.

There was no walking down the aisle, no rings exchanged, no wedding dress, and no music.

That all came several days later, when the pair had a bespoke ceremony led by a celebrant who knew them, at a venue in the Oxfordshire countryside. It was their dream wedding - but it wasn't legal in England and Wales.

And so in April, they forked out hundreds of pounds to quietly sign papers at a library in Buckingham.

"For us, that day was as insignificant as possible," Courtney told the BBC. "It was just the words we had to say to make it legally binding."

The Scholeys are one of a growing number of couples who feel the rigid rules around weddings are making getting married more stressful, more expensive and less meaningful.

But under new proposals announced this month - described by the government as the biggest shake-up of wedding laws in 200 years - couples in England and Wales could have the freedom to hold official marriage ceremonies in a wider array of unconventional locations, from forests to beaches, as long as the location is approved by a registered officiant.

It's welcome news for Nicky Brown, who said she wants to exchange vows in a wildly picturesque corner of Wales, with just her mum and her partner's mum as witnesses.

"I'd be quite happy to get married in a field full of sheep," the 57-year-old told the BBC.

But some say the sacred tradition of marriage is being perverted.

Currently, a marriage or civil partnership ceremony in England or Wales must take place at an approved venue to be legally binding – and many exert control on elements of the wedding such as vows, headcounts or music.

There are also tight restrictions on who can officiate a wedding and how. Authorised religious figures can, but – with few exceptions – only in places of worship.

Registrars can conduct a wedding, but it can't have any religious content. And celebrants can't legally marry people at all.

A Law Commission report in 2022 concluded that these marriage laws, which date back to the 18th and 19th Centuries, were "complicated, inefficient, unfair and needlessly restrictive".

David Lammy, then deputy prime minister, said marriage laws in England and Wales had "not kept pace with the social and cultural changes that have shaped modern Britain".

He added: "Some feel forced to pay for two different ceremonies, one legal and one belief based. Some enter into a marriage that isn't legally recognised. Others feel they have little choice but to marry in a way which doesn't reflect their beliefs, marring what should be a joyous occasion."

Scotland and Northern Ireland relaxed their rules years ago.

Though the exact shape of the new rules is still under public consultation until September, these changes will take regulations from a "buildings based" regulation model to an "officiant based" one.

Brown said she and her partner had put off getting married because there was no legal and affordable version of a wedding that reflects them.

She said she didn't want bells and whistles - or even a wedding dress. "I just want somebody to marry us and in a beautiful setting that isn't just going to cost the earth."

Brown went on to explain that she'd been scared her mum - who is 86 and unwell - would miss out on her wedding day. But these proposals had given her hope: "The laws are now, what, 200 years out of date?"

Miranda Allard, 66, agreed that change is long overdue.

When she got married 40 years ago, she had to jump through hoops to get permission to hold an interfaith ceremony in her parent's garden - and finds it astounding couples today face the same obstacles.

"We applied for a special licence... [and] explained how we did not want to put my Jewish mother-in-law through a church wedding," she said.

"I, on the other hand, was brought up in a Christian family and would not 'feel married' if doing so in a registry office."

It took letters from the couple, their parents, the local bishop, the village vicar and more to convince authorities to allow the ceremony.

"We also combined our legal Christian service with Jewish prayers and tradition, like breaking the glass. Totally unheard of then and ever since," she said, adding the nuptials even made the paper.

Father John, who didn't provide his last name, wrote in to BBC Your Voice to say he'd like to be able to perform ceremonies like this too.

"Marriage is about the lifelong commitment made before God for me, and for some couples the setting can make that sacred moment even more personal and memorable."

Brian Bracher, 65, from Chichester in West Sussex, said he cannot believe the UK is still debating these changes.

"It is ridiculous that, in this modern era, a small minority are still trying to exert control and make decisions about what is frivolous and not acceptable. Just let people, that love each other, marry in a way that suits them."

The proposals will be a welcome change for Christians from the LGBT community, said 33-year-old Isabel Sinagola.

She added: "[They] currently cannot have the wedding they might want, as they cannot marry in the Church of England, but also cannot have religious content in the only option available to them: a civil ceremony."

Others are hopeful this provides more affordable wedding options.

She says the changes won't take anything from those who still want traditional weddings – it simply gives couples who don't more options.

"You've got blended families, mixed cultures, traditions that are changing even within those cultures.

"Modern relationships deserve modern ceremonies."

The government has stressed there will be safeguards to guarantee the dignity of marriage is preserved.

Ceremonies deemed to be "gimmicks" that risk trivialising the legal act of marriage would not be allowed. Activities "such as skydiving, white-water rafting, roller coasters or other amusement rides" would "fall short of the standard".

"Every couple deserves to start their journey together with an unforgettable day that reflects their beliefs, their personalities and the lives they plan to build together," Lammy wrote.

"This Government's changes will bring weddings law into the twenty-first century."

GeneralTab.title: Faisal Islam: The UK's Trump trade deal no longer looks world-beating
GeneralTab.text:
It has been a long road for President Donald Trump as he looks for a justification to erect a tariff wall around the US, including against key allies.

From the opioid crisis to illegal migration, then the need to bring manufacturing back to America's shores, the list goes on.

Through Trump's second term, there has been a new justification almost every month for the trade levies he is seeking to place on allies.

Some have been overturned by the courts, others by economics and some even by their own logic. And so, Trump has now turned to effectively accusing dozens of trade partners of trading in goods that have been produced using forced labour.

These are "tariffs in search of an authority", as one industry figure put it. The forced labour line shores up President Trump's tariffs against a challenge from Congress or the courts.

In practice, the levies are curiously similar by country to a previous round of tariffs imposed supposedly for completely different reasons.

The good news for the UK is that the regime effectively remains the same as before.

What has changed is that our nearest neighbours in the European Union now have a much better deal than before, and in turn are in a better situation than the UK.

While the UK and the EU each appear to have a 10% rate, the EU's is a flat rate, while the UK's will apply alongside other tariffs, in a range of goods including footwear and textiles.

The government has struck effective side deals on medicines, steel, aluminium, cars and, with the help of King Charles, whisky.

At the end of this process however the overall trade-weighted effective tariff rate for the EU (8.5%) could end up a bit lower than the UK's (6.8%).

It should not matter that much, but the help given by doing the first deal, and by post-Brexit trade freedoms, looks to have been short-lived.

The British Chambers of Commerce trade expert William Bain points to the competitive advantage for EU exporters into the US in some sectors.

The EU has secured better treatment because it has passed a ban on forced labour goods, which the UK has not.

This is not an accusation on the use of forced labour in supply chains. It is about the passing of specific legislation, mirroring the US ban on products that have used forced labour in supply chains.

There should be scope for a better deal for the UK, but it raises an interesting question about whether the government will pursue an EU-style ban. This is widely seen as a backdoor way to target China, in particular for conditions in its Xinjiang province.

Last October, external the government said it "remained firmly opposed to the use of state-imposed forced labour", but that it was "considering how best to reflect this position," citing "operational and legal complexities".

Since then, the UK has welcomed imports of Chinese cars, and is exploring a services trade deal with the country. The relationship with China has been a balancing act for the government.

This is also one of the global stories of the tariff wars. As the US repeatedly changes its rationale for tariffs, the rest of the world is focused on trading with each other. For example, Canada increased its trade with the rest of the world by more than it lost from the US.

China's total dollar trade with the US is flat in the first half of this year versus last year. Across the world it is up 21%, including 14% with the EU, 11% with the UK, and 24% with Africa.

There could be pressure now to legislate for a formal ban on forced labour products. Successive governments have opted for a lighter voluntary due diligence regime.

Will the US force a change in the UK and elsewhere, and what might it offer in return?

Or the UK may opt to keep its precarious geopolitical position by sticking to its existing deals in medicines, metals and cars.

GeneralTab.title: UK mortgage rates rise to highest level for more than a month
GeneralTab.text:
UK average mortgage rates have risen back to the level of a month ago as renewed tensions in the Middle East feed through to homeowners.

Lenders' funding costs have increased as markets judge that a prolonged conflict reduces the possibility of interest rate cuts by central banks.

The five biggest High Street banks are among a host of lenders which have increased their interest rates on new fixed deals in recent days.

Recent projections by the Bank of England suggest just over five million homeowners should expect their monthly mortgage repayments to increase by the end of 2028.

Mortgage rates had been falling as a ceasefire between the US and Iran initially appeared to hold.

But fresh strikes and Houthi militia attacks on oil tankers in the Red Sea reignited fears over global energy supplies.

Oil prices hit $100 a barrel for the first time since May on Thursday after several days of increases, stoking fears of higher inflation and a lower likelihood of interest rate cuts.

More than eight in 10 mortgage customers have fixed-rate deals.

The interest rate on this kind of mortgage does not change until the deal expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it.

The average rate on a new two-year fixed deal is 5.59%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.

Although it has risen consistently in recent days and is the highest since 19 June, it remains below the Iran war peak in April of 5.9%.

The average rate on a five-year fixed deal is 5.61%, a level last seen on 7 June.

HSBC has also announced it will raise its mortgage rates on Monday.

"It will be incredibly frustrating for borrowers to see rates rise back up to where they were a month ago. The positive progress over recent weeks now feels all but lost, but what the market needs is a period of stability," said Rachel Springall, finance expert at Moneyfacts.

She said 100 deals had been pulled temporarily as lenders reconsider their pricing plans.

She suggested that anyone who needed to remortgage this year could lock in a new deal now with their existing lender ahead of time, but should also seek help from a broker to see whether there are better deals elsewhere.

"Brokers are an anchor during turbulent times as they can help borrowers keep abreast of changes and be there step by step when going through a mortgage application," she said.

Borrowers had been heartened by the regular falls in mortgage rates during June and early July, but brokers say the latest changes are evidence of the uncertainty in the sector.

"Any borrower hoping for rate cuts to become an ongoing trend will need to rethink," said David Hollingworth, of L&C Mortgages.

"Momentum has performed an about turn and now clearly shifted to fixed rates rising in the near term at least."

articles.title: Fleeing a wall of flames: Tourists describe France wildfires escape
articles.text:
Families have relived how their tranquil holidays in France turned into a race to escape raging wildfires.

Tourists told the BBC of emergency alerts in the middle of the night, desperate drives just metres from six-storey high flames and the sight of people flocking to beaches with their suitcases.

Huge forest fires in south-west France and central Spain have displaced more than 220,000 people, with the French military drafted in to help and the Spanish government declaring a national emergency.

Winds and continued heat are still helping to fan the flames with some tourists reporting smelling acrid smoke like a "bonfire" far outside the affected areas.

Flights to Bordeaux and Madrid, the closest cities to the blaze-hit regions, are currently not affected. Earlier on Saturday, a French foreign minister described the fires as a "tragedy" but urged tourists not to cancel their travel plans.

Among those caught up in the crisis is Zac Morrison, who arrived in Cap Ferret - a popular peninsula blanketed with pine trees 40 miles (65km) south-west of Bordeaux - on Thursday.

The 21-year-old from London, who is on holiday with 10 members of his family, woke up to two text alerts at 04:00 and 06:00 local time ordering him to evacuate "by all means necessary".

"We had the gendarmerie [French military] going door to door," he told BBC Your Voice. "It was something like out of a movie - we had to take everything."

Since experiencing "panic" before a "well organised" operation to clear out the entire peninsula, he said he received four different evacuation alerts from the authorities - the most recent at 17:00 on Friday - after "we moved away from one fire to only get put into the crosshairs of another".

His family took shelter on a beach in nearby Arcachon before a relative came to their aid with a place to stay. His brother Nate, 11, is still coming to terms with having seen the flames.

"Other people have been sleeping in schools and warehouses and the beaches have had people just waiting for the go ahead," Morrison added. "There's people on the beach here with their suitcases."

He said the family was awaiting instructions on whether they can continue their holiday until mid August.

"It rained last night but we are hearing that electricity may be cut out over the peninsula, especially as the ash clouds go towards Bordeaux... I've heard about houses burning in just an hour, it's scary but sadly people here are getting used to it."

David Morton had enjoyed most of his week-long trip to Cap Ferret with his wife and two teenage sons in the forests under baking sun.

But the mixture of "tinder dry" pine and intense heat helped upend things on day five when the family was awoken on Friday morning.

"Our phones were all flashing and bleeping; there was a message saying we had to evacuate immediately and drive on the one road out of the [Cap Ferret] peninsula," he said.

"We literally threw everything into our suitcases and within 15 minutes were in the hire car."

He said they came within 500m of the main fire. "The flames were higher than full-size forest pine trees, so five or six storeys high, and it was clear this was a fire that was out of control at that point."

The family has stayed with friends until their flight home from Bordeaux on Saturday.

Others are still stranded. Rebecca Papin, a French-American visiting her holiday home in the commune of Biscarrosse, near to the Cap Ferret peninsula, saw a large plume of smoke in the distance on Thursday.

Just three hours later when she arrived home that night, "there were water planes in the sky dropping water, firefighter helicopters in the sky and the entire distance was just a wall of flames," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

"It was quite far away from my house but I could see it very clearly from the upstairs level of my home."

She said the authorities appeared "overwhelmed with trying" to fight the fire and issued no evacuation order, so she slept alongside her young children with her earplugs in - meaning she missed the sound of the evacuation overnight.

"When I woke up in the morning we were almost alone in the city because the city has been evacuated and I'm still here," she said.

"The main roads are closed because they're on fire - the police advised me on Friday at 07:30 to stay in my home, to not leave my home under any circumstance; there was ash falling from the sky like snow."

Some British families told the BBC they had moved 100 miles away to other parts of France to continue their holidays.

Mark Dorey, from Leeds, decided to drive to the Dordogne with his wife and three children after being evacuated from a campsite near Parentis-en-Born.

"You wouldn't believe it, but me and my two boys were watching a Queen tribute act at the campsite bar - straight after a rendition of Bohemian Rhapsody someone stopped them to say we were being evacuated at about 22:00," he said.

Before heading to the Dordogne the family spent a night with hundreds of other evacuees in a gymnasium.

He said he feels lucky to be looked after and safe, but is thinking about holidaying "closer to home" next year.

And BBC South's Joanna Kent, who was on holiday in the Cap Ferret peninsula earlier this week, recalled seeing her campsite deserted after two van loads of police told tourists they had 30 minutes to get out.

While the wildfires show no sign of abating soon, the UK Foreign Office is currently not advising against travel to France or Spain.

Éléonore Caroit, France's minister for international partnerships, advised tourists on Saturday: "You have entire areas that are fine, you're seeing similar phenomena in Spain and other countries.

"I'm in Paris and nothing is happening, and most other regions are OK, so do please come to France and do not cancel your travel plans.

"But wherever you are, please do be advised as to what might be happening."

In Madrid the fires are in the wider region far outside the city centre - and authorities are battling to stop different fires merging.

But the flames have already shut down a facility for US space agency Nasa 37 miles (65km) west of the city.

Madrid's regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso described the fire there as the "worst fire in the history of the region", with the area facing a "perfect storm" of high temperatures, relentless wind and merging fire fronts.

Having been caught out, the force stepped up its efforts to investigate who was behind the illegal event, eventually arresting more than 40 people and charging 25, several of whom have now been convicted.

As officers tracked down the coursers, it turned out they had come from all over the country: Lincolnshire, Leicestershire, Berkshire, north Wales. "People had come hundreds of miles to be there that day," says Martin. "It was a proper operation."

Then, after searching an address belonging to one of the arrested men, police found the trophy the coursers had been competing for - the Super 8 Cup, etched with images of dogs and hares, standing maybe 2ft (61cm) tall, about the size of the FA Cup.

The invasion of Latta's farm had been a highlight of the illegal hare coursing calendar, a recurring cup competition whose previous winners are engraved on the base of the trophy - both the owners and the dogs, which had names such as "Beyoncé" and "Bunny".

A scene after the cup final last year, captured on video obtained by the BBC, shows how hare coursing involves serious money. A group of eight men can be seen drinking pints in a pub and shouting, as they haggle over a lurcher standing on the table before them. The dog was the Super 8 Cup champion of 2025 and sold for £55,000.

It is not the only evidence of the cash that flows through the illegal bloodsport: we were told the Super 8 Cup prize was about £50,000, while the entry fee for the competition was £1,000, as revealed by a seized phone belonging to one of the kingpins. Police say this cash funds the prize money and covers expenses, such as a pool of vehicles and even court costs in case the hare coursers are raided.

Ch Insp Kevin Lacks-Kelly, head of the UK National Wildlife Crime Unit, tells the BBC that money had also flowed into the illegal sport through livestreams for gamblers in China on one or two occasions. But he says the gangs in the UK did not need overseas bets to fund their illicit hobby.

Hare coursers were linked to crimes involving significant sums of money, says Lacks-Kelly, not "minimum-wage crimes". "Some of these lads are making a fortune. You've got some of the country's best organised criminals," he adds.

There are some localised events that still just involve a handful of men and dogs, Lacks-Kelly says, but the level of organisation in bigger events "has increased tenfold" with the influx of organised crime.

"They've got the advantage in numbers. And they will go anywhere and do anything and commit this crime at all costs," he says.

"They're like a small army, just do what they want, don't they? Turn up en masse, block roads off, drive over fields, cause damage, dump the cars, burn the cars out. Mass participation events that are designed to overwhelm."

The BBC contacted members of the Country Land and Business Association, which represents 30,000 rural landowners and businesses in England and Wales, to ask about their experiences with hare coursing.

About 50 responded, nearly all of them saying their land or property had been damaged. Someone in Cheshire said it happened every week, a farmer in Essex said it had happened more than 100 times, while one in North Yorkshire said 150 times.

And 29 of the respondents said they had been threatened with violence.

According to the survey responses, hare coursers had threatened to kidnap farmers' dogs, shouted that they would burn their buildings down, had thrown bricks through windows, made anonymous phone threats to stab them in the neck, used catapults to fire ball-bearings at them, rammed and damaged vehicles with people inside, and warned the farmers that they knew where they lived and where their kids go to school.

Wiltshire farmer David Lemon showed us his 3,000-acre farm, where hare coursers have previously torn up the fields with miles of tyre tracks. He has tried to fortify the land, closing off gateways, putting in concrete blocks or piles of logs, and digging rows of deep ditches to make it undrivable. But they still get in and, when he has tried to confront them, he has been threatened.

One gamekeeper was run over and badly injured when he tried to confront hare coursers on land he managed, says Tim Weston from the National Gamekeepers' Organisation.

"He broke both his legs, pelvis, ruptured lungs." Weston says. "They left at high speed, potentially could have left him for dead." Fortunately, the man is now back and work and recovering, he said.

As we talked, it turned out that Weston, who is now based in Wiltshire, grew up in a village near Broughton in Hampshire, where the animals were dumped outside the shop. In 2024, he was working in deer management on an estate where he suspects the dead hares had been killed.

The night before they were dumped, there had been wheel marks across the estate, he says. The local gamekeeper had stopped the hare coursers three or four times.

Weston says the abandoned animals were a message to say: "We've been. You didn't catch us this time."

Using dead animals to taunt landowners is common, Weston says. In our survey of farmers and landowners, 35 of the respondents said animal bodies had been deliberately left on their land.

It is a message to the local community that "we can do what we want because no-one's going to police it", Weston says.

Hampshire Police did arrest a man over the dumped animals at Broughton community shop, however. The force commissioned a forensic analysis of the dead kestrel and barn owl left on the doors and took DNA samples. James Kempster, a man who police say had a prior record of wildlife crimes, was arrested as a result.

At trial, Kempster denied he had abandoned the animals. CCTV footage of two men casually tossing dozens of dead hares outside the shop - one of them ripping one of the bodies in half to smear its blood around - were not clear enough to reveal their identities.

Kempster was convicted of handling the dead birds, a crime in itself because they are protected species. But he was found not guilty of criminal damage - the charge that related to abandoning the carcasses.

So was the incident really a warning or a taunt to the local community from hare coursers? With the perpetrators still unidentified, their motive cannot be known for certain.

One police officer recalls an arrangement of dead animals' whose message seemed undeniable, however. He tells us how he had sometimes found bodies strung over speed limit signs and street furniture in villages or left outside people's houses.

Once, he says, he had seen them laid out in the road, the corpses spelling out the words: "Catch me".

articles.title: Long overdue, life-changing or frivolous? Your thoughts on wedding rule changes
articles.text:
The day Sam and Courtney Scholey became husband and wife didn't feel like their wedding day.

There was no walking down the aisle, no rings exchanged, no wedding dress, and no music.

That all came several days later, when the pair had a bespoke ceremony led by a celebrant who knew them, at a venue in the Oxfordshire countryside. It was their dream wedding - but it wasn't legal in England and Wales.

And so in April, they forked out hundreds of pounds to quietly sign papers at a library in Buckingham.

"For us, that day was as insignificant as possible," Courtney told the BBC. "It was just the words we had to say to make it legally binding."

The Scholeys are one of a growing number of couples who feel the rigid rules around weddings are making getting married more stressful, more expensive and less meaningful.

But under new proposals announced this month - described by the government as the biggest shake-up of wedding laws in 200 years - couples in England and Wales could have the freedom to hold official marriage ceremonies in a wider array of unconventional locations, from forests to beaches, as long as the location is approved by a registered officiant.

It's welcome news for Nicky Brown, who said she wants to exchange vows in a wildly picturesque corner of Wales, with just her mum and her partner's mum as witnesses.

"I'd be quite happy to get married in a field full of sheep," the 57-year-old told the BBC.

But some say the sacred tradition of marriage is being perverted.

Currently, a marriage or civil partnership ceremony in England or Wales must take place at an approved venue to be legally binding – and many exert control on elements of the wedding such as vows, headcounts or music.

There are also tight restrictions on who can officiate a wedding and how. Authorised religious figures can, but – with few exceptions – only in places of worship.

Registrars can conduct a wedding, but it can't have any religious content. And celebrants can't legally marry people at all.

A Law Commission report in 2022 concluded that these marriage laws, which date back to the 18th and 19th Centuries, were "complicated, inefficient, unfair and needlessly restrictive".

David Lammy, then deputy prime minister, said marriage laws in England and Wales had "not kept pace with the social and cultural changes that have shaped modern Britain".

He added: "Some feel forced to pay for two different ceremonies, one legal and one belief based. Some enter into a marriage that isn't legally recognised. Others feel they have little choice but to marry in a way which doesn't reflect their beliefs, marring what should be a joyous occasion."

Scotland and Northern Ireland relaxed their rules years ago.

Though the exact shape of the new rules is still under public consultation until September, these changes will take regulations from a "buildings based" regulation model to an "officiant based" one.

Brown said she and her partner had put off getting married because there was no legal and affordable version of a wedding that reflects them.

She said she didn't want bells and whistles - or even a wedding dress. "I just want somebody to marry us and in a beautiful setting that isn't just going to cost the earth."

Brown went on to explain that she'd been scared her mum - who is 86 and unwell - would miss out on her wedding day. But these proposals had given her hope: "The laws are now, what, 200 years out of date?"

Miranda Allard, 66, agreed that change is long overdue.

When she got married 40 years ago, she had to jump through hoops to get permission to hold an interfaith ceremony in her parent's garden - and finds it astounding couples today face the same obstacles.

"We applied for a special licence... [and] explained how we did not want to put my Jewish mother-in-law through a church wedding," she said.

"I, on the other hand, was brought up in a Christian family and would not 'feel married' if doing so in a registry office."

It took letters from the couple, their parents, the local bishop, the village vicar and more to convince authorities to allow the ceremony.

"We also combined our legal Christian service with Jewish prayers and tradition, like breaking the glass. Totally unheard of then and ever since," she said, adding the nuptials even made the paper.

Father John, who didn't provide his last name, wrote in to BBC Your Voice to say he'd like to be able to perform ceremonies like this too.

"Marriage is about the lifelong commitment made before God for me, and for some couples the setting can make that sacred moment even more personal and memorable."

Brian Bracher, 65, from Chichester in West Sussex, said he cannot believe the UK is still debating these changes.

"It is ridiculous that, in this modern era, a small minority are still trying to exert control and make decisions about what is frivolous and not acceptable. Just let people, that love each other, marry in a way that suits them."

The proposals will be a welcome change for Christians from the LGBT community, said 33-year-old Isabel Sinagola.

She added: "[They] currently cannot have the wedding they might want, as they cannot marry in the Church of England, but also cannot have religious content in the only option available to them: a civil ceremony."

Others are hopeful this provides more affordable wedding options.

She says the changes won't take anything from those who still want traditional weddings – it simply gives couples who don't more options.

"You've got blended families, mixed cultures, traditions that are changing even within those cultures.

"Modern relationships deserve modern ceremonies."

The government has stressed there will be safeguards to guarantee the dignity of marriage is preserved.

Ceremonies deemed to be "gimmicks" that risk trivialising the legal act of marriage would not be allowed. Activities "such as skydiving, white-water rafting, roller coasters or other amusement rides" would "fall short of the standard".

"Every couple deserves to start their journey together with an unforgettable day that reflects their beliefs, their personalities and the lives they plan to build together," Lammy wrote.

"This Government's changes will bring weddings law into the twenty-first century."

Additional reporting by Mary Litchfield and Rozina Sini

articles.title: ADHD has rewired the workplace - these are the consequences
articles.text:
Taking one of the UK's biggest grocery chains to an employment tribunal was something that Ryan Toghill says almost took over his life.

"It was all I could think about for 18 months and more," he says.

The deputy store manager at Lidl, who'd told his bosses he'd been diagnosed with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), was called to a disciplinary meeting after breaking company rules by using equipment he hadn't been trained to use. After that meeting, Ryan was dismissed for gross misconduct.

He successfully appealed the decision and was offered a lower-paid role. He rejected it and took his case to a tribunal. Eventually, he was awarded more than £45,000 when the judge found his former employer hadn't fully taken his ADHD diagnosis into account during the disciplinary process.

The judgement found reasonable adjustments during the process hadn't been offered to him, such as additional breaks.

He'd been described by a manager as showing "a lack of remorse," something the tribunal found was clearly linked with his communication differences associated with having ADHD.

"I don't show a lot of emotions," Ryan explains. "I could be incredibly happy, angry, upset, or remorseful, and my facial expressions and tone of voice would essentially remain the same."

The tribunal upheld part of his claims for unfair dismissal, wrongful dismissal and a failure to make reasonable adjustments. Lidl says it's "committed to ensuring that everyone receives the reasonable adjustments, clear communication and support they need to thrive."

Campaigners, lawyers and HR teams say cases like this highlight a shift that businesses should be paying attention to.

Thousands of people have been diagnosed as neurodivergent in the last few years, an umbrella term that covers autism, ADHD and other conditions such as dyslexia and Tourette's syndrome.

Since the pandemic in particular, diagnosis rates for ADHD and autism have been rising, and they're featuring more regularly in disputes in employment tribunals.

While many people who are neurodivergent don't consider themselves disabled, the Equality Act 2010 may give them protection by recognising their condition as a disability, regardless of whether they have a formal diagnosis. They're entitled to reasonable adjustments if they can show that their condition has a substantial and long-term adverse effect on their ability to do normal day-to-day activities. These are widely defined and aren't limited to work tasks.

Cases going to tribunal can be around employers not making those adjustments, but they can also be about how people are treated at work.

For example, a 2025 tribunal found a software engineer who had ADHD had faced discrimination because a manager sighed and made other expressions of "non-verbal frustration" towards him.

"What we're seeing in tribunals is rarely the result of deliberate discrimination," says Lutfur Ali, a diversity and inclusion adviser at the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development, the professional body for HR.

"Cases commonly stem from reasonable adjustments being overlooked, performance processes that were never designed with different thinking styles in mind, and managers lacking confidence because they haven't been given the training or the time to have the right conversations."

So, while awareness of neurodivergence has never been higher, why are more cases like this ending up in the legal system? And are businesses struggling to keep up with the needs of the workforce?

Irwin Mitchell is one of the biggest law firms in the UK, and its lawyers say their caseloads increasingly include grievances linked to neurodivergence at work.

Using the Ministry of Justice's online judgments database, the company identified 517 employment tribunal cases mentioning neurodivergent conditions in 2025, up from 265 in 2020. The most commonly cited conditions were autism and ADHD.

The live database is limited and gives only a partial picture. The Ministry of Justice says the figures should not be considered official statistics.

Diagnosis rates of ADHD and autism have soared, and waiting lists for assessments on the NHS in England are at record levels, with lists even closing in some areas due to the huge demand. Irwin Mitchell says those long waits have an impact on workplaces too. "Anecdotally, we're seeing a lot of people that are either threatening to bring claims or actually bringing claims, that don't have formal diagnoses," says Jo Moseley, a legal director at the firm.

Similarly, research by King's College London last year suggested that around 90% of autistic people over 40 remain undiagnosed.

Diagnosis levels aside, there has been a huge increase in awareness of the challenges neurodivergent people can face - whether it's in communication preferences, personal organisation, or sensory needs. In workplaces, many describe "masking," a term which means trying to hide their traits in order to fit in - something which can put a huge strain on the person's wellbeing.

"Society is playing catch-up," says Ben Branson, an entrepreneur who runs a charity called The Hidden 20%, which campaigns for better understanding of neurodivergence. He was diagnosed with autism in 2022.

"The recognition of adult neurodivergence has exploded," he says. "But we have always been here, we are just not hiding anymore, and there are millions of people finally understanding why they kept moving jobs, why they didn't fit, why they kept burning out and why they felt so exhausted, who are no longer willing to struggle in silence."

This year's City and Guilds Foundation's Neurodiversity Index found that while employers think they're "doing better" when it comes to inclusion, neurodivergent employees say they are seeing only small improvements.

This disconnect between managers and staff is something employment lawyer Jodie Hill is familiar with. Her firm, Thrive Law, specialises in workplace wellbeing and works with both employees and businesses. She set it up in 2018 after getting her own ADHD diagnosis at the age of 35.

"In the last three months, I've seen more than I've ever seen before in terms of enquiries," she says.

So, what are some employers doing that leads to successful action being taken against them? Hill says one thing that comes up a lot is bosses asking for proof of a formal diagnosis, when this isn't the legal test. Another issue can be an employer looking to dismiss someone over performance before considering a possible disability. Both of which could leave them exposed to claims of discrimination.

In the training sessions she carries out for businesses, she says she hears from the employer's perspective that it can feel like "every other conversation is about people wanting support".

Fears over cost, and concern that doing something for one member of staff means they have to do it for all of them, can lead to what Hill describes as an "initial dismissiveness" from some employers. But that, she says, comes from a lack of understanding over what can be an "internal and invisible" struggle.

"There's a mindset from employers that it's very linear… and that all the symptoms are the same every day," she says.

Another challenge can be determining what constitutes a "reasonable adjustment," a sticking point which can be what ends up being decided in a tribunal.

Hill says some employers "don't know where to start" and wrongly assume that making reasonable adjustments means doing whatever the employee asks.

Some tribunals have shown the limits of what's "reasonable." In one case, an autistic claimant had requested extensive changes to the recruitment process at the Judicial Appointments Commission (JAC), including simplified questions and advance access to test questions. The JAC had already offered extra time and assistance from a friend and denied the extra requests. When it went to tribunal, the judge found the adjustments the person had asked for were "clearly going beyond what was necessary or reasonable".

While there isn't a check list for employers, lawyers stress that they have to be able to justify why they're saying no to something, and show they've looked at alternative options.

Jo Moseley from law firm Irwin Mitchell explains that when it comes to judging what is "reasonable", a tribunal would take into account factors like the person's role, and the size of the business.

"Big employers will certainly be expected to do more than small employers," she says, stressing that many adjustments can cost nothing or very little, such as looking at how meetings are structured, offering regular breaks, or somewhere quiet to work.

In one tribunal last year, the pub chain Greene King was found to have failed to make reasonable adjustments for a chef who was dyslexic and struggled with reading orders.

He'd asked for a Bluetooth headset. The tribunal found that the company's failure to provide this adjustment had led to his employment ending. He was awarded £24,000. A spokesperson for Greene King said it respected the tribunal's decision and that it was committed to upholding the highest standards of employee welfare.

"Ultimately, the purpose of an adjustment is to facilitate good performance, not to lower the standard of performance," says Prof Nancy Doyle, an occupational psychologist.

"Employers are anxious of challenge, anxious about saying or doing the wrong thing," she adds.

She explains that employers are not expected to keep someone in a job where they're risking safety or delivering less than their peers, but that in some workplaces, managers end up "covering for neurodivergent staff," leaving them in a situation where they are "dependent on kindness, which may ebb away over time."

Daniel Rickman, who runs glazing business Structura, decided not to wait for individuals to ask for adjustments - but instead offer them to all staff.

The company introduced flexible working, fidget toys in meeting rooms, and red or green "busy lights" on desks, that allow staff to indicate whether they're happy to be disturbed.

He says it means the business is "getting the best out of everybody" and he is retaining skilled staff. However, showing the polarisation around the topic, he says he has also been criticised for being "woke."

As awareness of neurodiversity has grown, some businesses such as Microsoft and BAE Systems have created targeted hiring programmes to attract neurodivergent candidates, aware of the skills they can bring to their organisations.

Making neurodiversity a part of how workplaces are designed is what Prof Amanda Kirby believes is needed.

She's heading up the government's expert panel, set up to look at improving the job chances of neurodivergent people, and says a "medical" model of providing adjustments is inadequate.

"Nobody fits into neat boxes", she says, adding that training focused on doing x for dyslexia or y for ADHD is "never going to work."

"It's not neurodiversity over here, mental health over here, unemployment over there," she says, pointing out that those who are not in employment, education or training, and those moving through the justice system are less likely to have a diagnosis and more likely to be neurodivergent.

Kirby's report is yet to be published, but it's part of the government's wider plans to tackle stubborn levels of economic inactivity that remain higher than before the pandemic.

A Government report in 2024 found autistic graduates are twice as likely to be unemployed after 15 months as non-disabled graduates, and last year, the government's ADHD Taskforce estimated that "unsupported" ADHD was costing the economy £17bn a year.

The latest official figures show the number of people receiving Personal Independent Payments topping 4 million, the number of those with ADHD as their main condition was around 100,000 in April, up by 30,000 in the last two years. Just over half of these were aged 16 to 24.

The government is investing £3.5bn into personalised employment support for disabled people and those with health conditions in order to address problems with employment levels.

A Department for Work and Pensions spokesperson told the BBC: "For too long disabled people and those with a neurodiversity condition have been left behind, ignored, and not given the support they need to get into work."

As well as costly, these tribunal claims are becoming increasingly drawn out as the UK's tribunal system creaks.

Figures from the Ministry of Justice put the number of open claims at a record high of 531,000.

Jenna Ide, a partner and employment law specialist at Thomas Mansfield Solicitors, says that the backlog adds pressure on employers.

"It can take several years for a case to reach a final hearing," she says. "In the meantime, employers are often required to make difficult judgement calls without knowing where a tribunal would ultimately draw the line," she adds.

Law firms say some tribunals are now being listed for 2030 and the backlog is expected to grow with the Employment Rights Act. From January 2027, this will give workers protection against unfair dismissal after six months instead of only after two years.

"Most people, even conservatively, think that there's going to be a huge explosion just in unfair dismissal claims," says Irwin Mitchell's Jo Moseley.

Not only could this backlog create problems in terms of access to justice, but according to Kirby, rising numbers of tribunals could have another troubling effect.

"Some employers will go, 'these people' are potentially going to cause us lots of problems," she says, adding that this could lead to a "hidden bias" in recruitment, where employers consider it too risky to take on someone they believe to be neurodivergent and so find a reason to give the job to someone else.

Ryan Toghill, who says he hasn't worked since leaving Lidl because of poor health, says his experience has left him conflicted over whether he would tell a prospective employer about his diagnosis.

But despite the challenges, his hope is that workplace changes will "trickle through businesses" in time.

"You've got to manage people differently if they're neurodivergent," he says. "You can get the best out of them, if you adapt a little bit."

articles.title: Police declare 'major incident' over Nethy Bridge wildfire
articles.text:
A major incident has been declared by emergency services as they continue to tackle a wildfire which has been burning in the Cairngorms National Park for 10 days.

Some residents of the village of Nethy Bridge have been evacuated as a precaution.

But a local resident told the BBC the wildfire should have been declared a major incident sooner and communication from authorities had been "pretty poor".

The Scottish government said a fire break had been established around Nethy Bridge overnight and new fire breaks were being constructed.

First Minister John Swinney, who held a meeting of the Scottish government's resilience committee early on Saturday, said additional police and fire service resources were being deployed to assist with the evacuation.

He said that it was "essential people avoid the affected areas."

Swinney continued: "The wind has changed direction overnight, which means the track of the fire has altered once again and the threat to Nethy Bridge has reduced, for the moment at least.

"Ground and helicopter resources are being focused on the current path of the fire and new fire breaks constructed."

Smoke from the wildfire can now be seen 59 miles away in Aberdeen following a change in wind direction.

He said they decided to stay unless the fire got considerably closer, adding: "We've got a camper van and we're all ready and set to go at a moment's notice. If it gets smoky, we'll go."

A wedding was due to take place at Castle Roy, which is near the village, but Eccles said this has had to be cancelled as a result of the wildfire evacuations.

He said the Scottish government's response had been "poor" and a major incident should have been declared earlier, with military assistance brought in to tackle the fire before it spread.

Eccles said: "It's a bit like closing the stable door now that the horse has bolted."
